On common sense

Today, while reversing my trailer full of scoria, i ran over some drainage pipe i bought yesterday.  oops.  Two days ago i used my digger to tilt my trailer full of sand, and snapped the trailer's brake cable. 

While I remain very aware of the current batch of AIs lack of 'common sense' and the ability to really 'self-doubt' (although we are now definitely seeing hints of meta-cognition in r1 and o3), I wonder if an upcoming AI, interfaced to some camera-toting head-up-display smart glasses might be a very good investment! 

Imagine an AI always looking out for the things you might have not noticed yourself that might be a safety or idiot issue. 

This ties in nicely with my suspicion that AIs with common sense will be dual in some essential way, each side challenging the other during active reasoning, the way my brain glitches on more that most.

But it's good to here Sam Altman increasingly talking about the limitations of even future AIs along the same lines.

Addendum: I want my AI to do my internet arguing for me.  But Sam seems to be saying that this feature isn't coming soon.  /sigh

The whole "1 person billion $ company" I think is poorly thought out. The problem with AI is the same as with something like movies. comments.author: @KevinColin-co9io
comments.text:
The argument that open-sourcing AGI is too dangerous for the "average person" is a smokescreen for maintaining control. While framed as a safety measure, it ignores that malicious actors already possess the means and motivation to misuse advanced technology, regardless of accessibility. Restricting access won't stop them; it might even hinder oversight.
Furthermore, the "average person" narrative overestimates the capacity for harm. Running AGI locally will likely remain resource-intensive. Knowing how to create something dangerous is vastly different from having the infrastructure and expertise to manufacture it at scale. The focus on individual misuse distracts from the greater danger: the concentration of AGI power.
Closed AGI centralizes control in the hands of a few, creating immense power imbalances. This fosters surveillance capitalism on steroids, information manipulation, and unequal access to AGI's benefits. "Security through obscurity" is a fallacy. Secrecy can hide vulnerabilities, while open-sourcing allows broader expert scrutiny, potentially enhancing safety through collective oversight and faster risk identification.
Closed AGI also stifles innovation and limits societal benefit. Open access could democratize research, accelerate safety breakthroughs, and foster diverse applications across various fields. Open-sourcing acts as a "sandbox for safety," enabling collaborative improvement and risk mitigation.
The real agenda behind calls for closed AGI isn't public safety, but power consolidation. We should shift focus from futile access prevention to mitigating risks through ethical frameworks, global collaboration, and AI safety research. True safety lies not in control, but in transparency, shared responsibility, and empowering a wider community to shape AGI's future. Openness, with appropriate safeguards and ethical guidelines, may be the more robust and beneficial path forward than centralized control masked as protection.

Disclaimer: google models helped me structure this argument😅😅

I know the technology will improve, I'm just thinking of the early days of these experiments.
